title: Hanukkah: show the light
hookLine: the lights go where passers-by can see

lines: A GLASS BOX BY THE DOOR.
cards: An early winter evening, a street of houses and apartments. In one window, a row of small flames. In another, a little glass box by the front door, with oil lamps inside.
On an apartment balcony, electric bulbs. Plenty of what happens in a Jewish home stays inside, among family. These lights are different.
They're placed so that someone walking past, who may not know or care what they mean, can see them. And there's a rule behind that, with a two-word name.

teach.b: Pirsumei nisa is Aramaic. It means publicizing the miracle, and it sits behind many of the rules about where and when the Hanukkah lights are lit.
The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the lamp should be set at the entrance of the house, on the outside.

teach.h: AT THE DOOR, FACING THE STREET.
teach.b: If you live upstairs, you place it in a window facing the public street.
Its time is from when the sun goes down until the last people have gone home from the market, because that's when the street is full of people to see it.
You may not even use the Hanukkah light for anything practical, like reading. That's one reason for the extra candle, the shammash, the helper: you use that one, and the others are just for showing.

teach.h: IN DANGER, THE TABLE IS ENOUGH.
teach.b: In a time of danger, the Talmud says, it's enough to set the lamp on your table inside.
Showing the light matters, but not more than a life. Families in dangerous times and places have done exactly that, lighting quietly, indoors.

In safer times and places the lights came back out to the windows, and in some cities to giant public lamps in town squares. The principle is the same in every case: a miracle that stays private isn't finished being told.
The lights are meant to be noticed, and the person who notices doesn't have to be Jewish, or even curious. They just have to walk by.

how: Families light the Hanukkah menorah at nightfall, adding one light each night, and place it by the door or in a window facing the street so passers-by can see; many communities also hold public menorah lightings.

games.q: it's a dangerous time and place to be seen as Jewish. it's the first night of Hanukkah. where does the Talmud say to put the lamp?
games.why: in a time of danger, it's enough to set it on your table. publicizing the miracle matters, but not more than a life.

practice: Look back over the last week and find one good thing: a kindness someone did for you, a worry that turned out fine, a small win. Picture who might like to hear it.
Then sit with the good thing itself, quietly, like a flame in a window.

wordCard.voice: Pirsumei nisa. Publicizing the miracle: the reason the Hanukkah lights face the street. Today's word.
